Okay, so let's start class. Today we are doing the Bronze Age collapse. Let's review where we are in history. Remember the four earlier civilizations: Egypt, Mesopotamia, Indus Valley, and China. These were the first major civilizations because they had major rivers that allowed them to develop agriculture and trade overseas. In these civilizations, a major city would emerge with colonies along the river. In Egypt, it's the Nile; in Mesopotamia, the Euphrates and Tigris; in China, the Yellow River; and in the Indus Valley, the Indus River.

These different city-states would go to war to control trade routes, leading to a time of major innovation. Because of these wars, they needed better equipment, which eventually led to the development of bronze. Bronze is an alloy of tin and copper—both are necessary for creating this strong metal ideal for shields, armor, and swords. Whoever had more bronze weaponry would win any war.

However, tin was hard to mine and discover. Tin deposits were scattered all over the world: here, there, everywhere. To access tin, more trade routes developed, turning major points of trade into cities themselves. This globalized world facilitated warfare but also brought the Indus Valley into this system. Archaeology in modern-day Pakistan has not discovered weaponry from the Indus Valley; we have found bronze but no weapons. We believe that in this valley, it was a peaceful, egalitarian, and artistic civilization, yet it was still part of this global system because bronze changed from weaponry to status, used for pottery, jewelry, and eventually as capital.

This world was heavily globalized, with extensive trading and complete, touching every corner of the globe. Starting around 1200 BCE, this system collapsed suddenly and devastatingly. In Chinese history, this marks the fall of the Shang dynasty. During this time, Egypt faced attacks by the Sea Peoples, who we believe were refugees fleeing Europe due to a perfect storm: climate change leading to drought, famine, and migration.

This perfect storm wiped out existing civilizations including Minoan Greece and the Hittite Empire in Anatolia (modern-day Turkey), where Troy is located—central to global trade. The fall of Minoan Greece and the Hittite Empire as major antagonists explains why people fought over the location of Troy, which was crucial in the Trojan War.
